source.title: Forecasting Side Effects of Activation Steering
source.authors: Yong-Ong Chong; A. Sim; Pei-Xin Zhang; Jun Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study measures activation-steering side effects and tests whether similarity between behavior steering directions predicts them. It does not test feature superposition, sparse co-activation, feature capacity, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. The direction-geometry results below concern a related but different construct.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about steering-direction geometry and behavioral cross-effects, not whether sparse features are stored as overlapping directions. Table 5 results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. Cited results and values used only for selecting layers, coefficients, or hyperparameters are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures side effects of difference-of-means activation steering across 67 judged behaviors and tests whether cosine similarity between steering directions predicts them. It does not examine sparse features vs. dimensions, polysemantic neurons, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. It does not mention superposition; its only link is the linear representation hypothesis as a framing. Its direction-geometry results concern a related but different construct (behavior steering directions and cross-effects), so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that steering side effects are pervasive, low-dimensional and often asymmetric. Direction-similarity heuristics explain at most about 23% of coupling. A propagation map plus linear probes forecasts side-effect direction (68–78% sign accuracy on the top decile) better than cosine baselines. Effect magnitude is mostly determined by the target behavior.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses difference-of-means activation steering on LLMs; it does not reproduce or test the toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction-similarity prediction varies by model and metric: whitening is best on the Gemma models, while raw cosine is best on Qwen2.5-7B. Removing the leading component also changes results differently across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine similarity between behavior steering directions explains little held-out cross-effect variance. Raw cosine gives R² +0.061/+0.009/+0.194; the best variant gives +0.215/+0.232/+0.194. Removing the top shared component collapses the best variant to +0.005/+0.032/+0.029.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric overlap of behavior steering directions is a weak, model-dependent predictor of behavioral interference under steering, carried largely by one shared component.

fits_no_version.finding: The cross-effect matrix is low-dimensional: participation ratio 4.6–4.9 vs. 23–26 for shuffled nulls, with one elaboration-vs-terseness mode carrying about 64% of variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering side effects across behaviors are dominated by a few shared interaction modes.

record.problems: The geometry results concern behavioral steering directions and side-effect prediction, not feature storage. The study notes that matrices are single-judge, human rating validation is limited, and findings establish consistency under the judges rather than absolute ground truth.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected related-geometry results. Other reported side-effect forecasts and steering outcomes were excluded because they do not measure feature superposition, feature capacity, SAE units, or feature dimensionality.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity sweep or feature geometry.
All: no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
All: no neuron distribution or SAE recovery of features.
All: steering uses single directions by construction. A subspace-overlap diagnostic is called non-causal and is not a test of feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: I changed relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only' because superposition is never discussed; the only related framing is a citation of the linear representation hypothesis. The rows are correctly unlinked. r6 duplicates r3. The study does not bear on any superposition version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse feature counts relative to dimensions, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or recoverable by an SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
